name: WebOTP (one time code from SMS)
plain: Lets a page read the one time code from an SMS the person receives.
meaning: Reads one matching SMS code that is tied to the site's domain; not the whole SMS inbox.

access.prompt_ui: Bottom sheet on Android to allow code sharing
access.iframe: Same as top level; cross-origin iframes need a permissions policy where listed

safari.note: Safari 27 has otp_option member; OTPCredential absent

data.metric: Lets a page read the one time code from an SMS the person receives.

limits.headline: Can see one text message code meant for that site, after you allow it
limits.user_action: You ask to log in or confirm a phone number, then tap Allow on the sheet
can: Receive the one time code from a text message that names the site's web address
Fill in that code for you, so you do not type it
Ask again each time a new code arrives
cannot: Receive a code from a message that does not name the site
Work on iPhone, Safari or Firefox
Keep watching for codes after you leave the page
limits.differs: Works in Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet on Android. Safari and Firefox do not support it; iPhone shows the code as a keyboard suggestion instead.

story.what_it_is: A page can read the six digit code from a text message so you do not have to type it.

marketing.name: WebOTP API
marketing.pitch: Automatically fills the verification code from an SMS, so signing in on the web is faster.

marketing.name: WebOTP API
marketing.pitch: A way for a page to receive a one time password from a text message, with the person's consent.

story.for_you: You get a text with a code. Your browser shows a small box asking if the site may use it. You tap Allow and the code drops into the form, so you skip copying digits.
story.for_makers: Fewer people give up at sign in or payment. The text uses a special format that names the site's own domain, so only that site can read the code. This lifts sign up rates and cuts support calls.

use_cases.example: You log in to a bank's web page, get a text, and the code fills in after one tap.
You pay online and the card bank texts a one time code. A checkout page reads it so you do not leave the page.
A shopping site sends a code when you create an account. Chrome on Android offers to fill it, so signup takes seconds.
You open a ride booking site on your phone and verify your number. The code fills itself, so you get a car faster.
A web social app verifies a new phone number during signup without making you leave the browser to read a text.
A site uses it to make two step sign in easier, which makes people more willing to turn it on.
A browser game with phone login lets you verify your number and get back to playing in one tap.

risks: Texts can be hijacked by SIM swap

technical_bounds: SMS must contain a bound domain line
No desktop SMS without paired Android

abuse: Phishing sites without matched domain fail

history.change: Desktop Chrome with Android phone as sync source
Safari 27 adds an otp_option member only
